problem: Section 1 defines T as a map from moving-image coordinates to fixed-image coordinates, and the aligned image as M(T⁻¹(x)). The SSD and NCC formulas then write M(T_θ(x)) for a point x on the fixed grid. With the stated direction, T_θ(x) is a coordinate in the fixed image, so sampling M there compares F(x) with the wrong point of M; the two conventions contradict each other inside one chapter.
fix: Keep the Section 1 direction and write SSD(θ) = Σ_x [F(x) − M(T_θ⁻¹(x))]² and NCC = Σ_x (F(x)−F̄)(M(T_θ⁻¹(x))−M̄) / √(Σ_x (F(x)−F̄)² Σ_x (M(T_θ⁻¹(x))−M̄)²), with the note that M(T_θ⁻¹(x)) is the moving intensity sampled at the moving coordinate that lands on fixed pixel x. (Equivalently, declare once that T maps fixed to moving and use M(T_θ(x)) everywhere plus T⁻¹ for resampling, but do not mix the two.)

where: Section 1 formula, Section 3 resampling and Dice
problem: The symbol A is reused three times: the 2×2 affine matrix in Section 1, the aligned image A(x) in Section 3, and one of the two label masks in the Dice formula. A student skimming will lose track of which A is meant.
fix: Use distinct letters: keep A for the affine matrix, write the aligned image as W(x) = M(T_θ⁻¹(x)), and write Dice = 2|P∩Q|/(|P|+|Q|) for label masks P and Q.

problem: "RANSAC is robust because one bad match cannot pull the fit far" is misleading. A single bad match inside a minimal sample ruins that whole hypothesis, and a bad match that survives into the final inlier set does bias the refit. RANSAC works because bad hypotheses get few inliers and are thrown away, not because a bad match has little influence.
fix: Say: RANSAC is robust because each hypothesis is fitted from a minimal sample, so an outlier usually lands in a sample whose inlier count is low, and that hypothesis is discarded; the final transform is refitted only on the inlier set.
